newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-PENALTY DECISION IGNITES OLD CONTROVERSIES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PENALTY DECISION IGNITES OLD CONTROVERSIES.

text.p: Real Zaragoza have appealed against a hotly-disputed penalty decision and sending off which helped Barcelona turn around a deficit and go on to score a 5-3 victory on Sunday.

The incident looks like igniting old suspicions over the refereeing of games involving the country's leading clubs and may even influence how much referees listen to their linesmen, and the kind of language they use.

With twenty minutes left to play and the home side leading 3-2, referee Manuel Mejuto sent off Zaragoza's Xavier Aguado and awarded Barcelona a penalty on the strength of advice given to him by a linesman.
Television and radio viewers have been treated to an unexpurgated version of the conversation -- complete with heavy swearing -- captured by a special microphone.
"What number?" asks referee Enrique Mejuto at one stage.
"For me, it's number six," says linesman Rafael Guerrero, refering to Aguado.
Television replays suggested that Barcelona's Fernando Couto had been pushed from behind in an off-the-ball incident, but that Jesus Solana was the man responsible.
Solana later denied he had been involved in anything more than routine pushing and said that Couto -- who fell to the ground -- had overreacted.
"If it had happened in the Barcelona area, I'm not sure the referee would have been as brave," said Zaragoza manager Victor Fernandez, in language more measured than that used by most of his players.
With 1,500 angry fans waiting outside the stadium, the match officials had to be given a police escort from the ground an hour after the game.
Zaragoza officials say they will up the matter with the Spanish League and viewpoints of the incident were reflected by contrasting coverage in the Zaragoza and Barcelona press.
In Zaragoza readers woke up to headlines such as "Scandal" and "Robbery", while the decision was relegated to the inside pages of Barcelona's newspapers.
"The braveness of the referee, sending off Aguado and awarding the penalty, was decisive," commented the Barcelona "Sport" daily.
Referees are frequently accused of favouring Barcelona and especially Real Madrid, the "grandees" of the Spanish game.
In a country addicted to soccer scandal, grumbling over decisions periodically ignites into full-scale accusations of bias.
Consistent complaints have led Spanish football authorities to choose match officials by ballot.

Already this season outspoken Atletico Madrid owner Jesus Gil complained that his defenders are more harshly dealt with than Barcelona players, while Deportivo Coruna coach John Toshack suggested that the problems at Real Madrid would mean that referees would be more inclined to favour them.
